q.q: What is e-safety?
o: A type of anti-virus software for phones
The safe and responsible use of technology
A setting that blocks unsuitable websites
The rules for using computers in school only
q.why: E-safety (online safety) is the safe, responsible and ethical use of technology.

q.q: Which of these is an example of e-safety being about behaviour rather than electronic security?
o: Setting a password on your phone
Keeping your apps up to date
Thinking about how you treat others before you post
Installing anti-virus software on your laptop
q.why: E-safety is as much about behaviour (how you treat others, what you share, who you trust) as about security.

q.q: What percentage of 8–17 year olds said someone they know shared a photo or video of them without asking?
q.why: 52% said this; 81% know how to ask permission and 47% think fitting in online is important.

q.q: Which of these does e-safety cover?
o: The internet, texts, gaming, email and smart devices
Only social networks such as TikTok and Snapchat
Only computers and laptops used in school
Only websites viewed in a browser on a computer
q.why: E-safety covers the internet and other electronic communication: texts, messaging, gaming, email and smart devices.

q.q: What does privacy mean?
o: Only using the internet when nobody else is around
Never using the internet at all
Deleting every post after one day
Keeping control of your personal information and who can see it
q.why: Privacy means keeping control of your personal information and who can see it.

q.q: About how many 11–13 year olds have broadcast themselves live on the internet?
o: Nearly 1 in 3
Nearly 1 in 2
Nearly 1 in 10
Nearly all of them
q.why: Nearly 1 in 3 11–13 year olds have live-streamed themselves.

q.q: Why is live streaming yourself risky?
o: It slows down the internet for others
It uses up all your storage
It can only be seen by your friends
Anyone watching can record it
q.why: Once it's out, a live stream can be recorded by anyone watching.

q.q: You want to post a photo of your friend from a party. What should you do first?
o: Ask your friend's permission
Post it, then delete it if they complain
Tag them so they get a notification
Add a filter so they are harder to recognise
q.why: Always ask before posting a photo or video of someone else.

q.q: Which of these is the highest risk to post online?
o: Your favourite film
Your favourite colour
Your home address
Your favourite game genre
q.why: Your address lets strangers find your exact home.

q.q: Why is a photo of you in your school uniform risky to post?
o: It uses too much mobile data
It shows which school you go to
It breaks school copyright rules
Uniform photos cannot be deleted
q.why: The uniform and badge show which school you go to, so someone could find you there.

q.q: Orla posts a selfie with her live location attached while she is at the park. Why is this high risk?
o: Someone could see exactly where she is and come to find her
It shows which school she goes to
It lets people guess her password
It will use up her phone's data allowance
q.why: Geotagging shows exactly where you are right now, so someone could come and find you.

q.q: What is the golden rule for personal information?
o: Post it only once
Share it only with online friends
Put it in your profile bio
Keep it private
q.why: The golden rule is KEEP IT PRIVATE, including online.

q.q: What is personal information?
o: Information that could identify you or help someone find or contact you
Information about your favourite games, films and music only
Information that only your parents and family know about you
Any information at all that you post on a social network
q.why: Personal information could identify you, or help someone find or contact you.

q.q: Why is giving out your mobile phone number high risk?
o: It lets the phone company charge you extra for every message you get
Strangers can contact you directly and privately, away from the app's safety tools
It lets strangers work out your school and town from the area code
It will be shown to everyone on your profile and next to your avatar
q.why: Strangers can contact you directly, privately, at any time, away from the platform's safety tools.

q.q: Why is sharing your date of birth and full name high risk?
o: They show exactly where you are right now
They can be used to steal your identity and guess passwords
They let strangers call you at any time
They tell people which school you go to
q.why: Date of birth and full name can be used to steal your identity, guess passwords and find you on other sites.

q.q: Sharing your favourite video game genre is low risk. Why is it not completely safe?
o: Groomers can use shared interests to build trust
It is personal information that identifies you
It lets people guess your phone number
It shows exactly where you live
q.why: It doesn't identify or locate you, but groomers can use shared interests to build trust.

q.q: Why can several small, low-risk details still be a problem?
o: They make your account load slowly
They are always shared with advertisers
They take up too much storage space
They can be pieced together to find you
q.why: First name + football club + a photo outside your house can be pieced together to find you.

q.q: Which question should you ask before you share anything online?
o: Will this get more likes than my last post did?
Could a stranger use this to find me, contact me or pretend to be me?
Is this the funniest thing I could post today?
Have my friends already posted something like this?
q.why: If a stranger could use it to find, contact or impersonate you, keep it private.

q.q: What is an avatar?
o: A picture or character used instead of your real photo
A setting that hides your location from strangers
A private message sent to just one friend
A list of the people who follow your account
q.why: An avatar represents you without showing your face.

q.q: Why shouldn't you post that you're on holiday while you're away?
o: Holiday photos use too much data
It's against the law to post abroad
Your friends might be jealous
People know your house is empty
q.why: Burglars could find out your home is empty.

q.q: Why is it a good idea to keep your profile private?
o: So you get more friend requests
So only real friends and family can see it
So your posts load faster
So strangers can find you easily
q.why: Privacy settings give you control over who sees your profile.

q.q: A 'friend of a friend' you have never met sends you a friend request. What should you do?
o: Decline, because you don't know who they really are
Accept, because your friend knows them
Accept, but don't reply to their messages
Ask them to send a photo to prove who they are
q.why: Only accept friends you know in real life.

q.q: How long can a photo posted online stay there?
o: Forever
Only until you delete it
Only until your account is closed
Only for 24 hours
q.why: Photos posted online are there for ever, because others can copy and share them.

q.q: Which test do the notes suggest before posting a photo?
o: Is it the clearest photo you have taken?
Has it got enough likes on another app?
Does it show your face from the front?
Would you be happy for your granny or teacher to see it?
q.why: Never post photos you wouldn't want your granny or your teacher to see.

q.q: Why might a silly photo from when you were young affect you later?
o: Photos are deleted after five years
Old photos make your account run slowly
Employers often look up people's social media
Schools charge for photos of pupils
q.why: Employers often look up people's social media, and silly photos could affect whether you get a job.

q.q: Someone you met online asks you to send them a photo of yourself. What should you do?
o: Never send photos to strangers
Send one, then delete it from your phone
Send one with your face blurred
Send one only if they send one first
q.why: Never send photos to strangers; once sent you lose control of it.

q.q: What is griefing?
o: Deliberately spoiling other players' games
Playing a game offline in airplane mode
Buying skins and extra currency
Feeling upset after losing a game
q.why: Griefing is deliberately spoiling other players' games through harassment or cheating.

q.q: Ryan's parents get a large bill after he buys skins and currency in a game. Which risk of online gaming is this?
o: Griefing
In-game purchases
Strangers
Offensive chat
q.why: Games encourage you to buy extras like skins and currency, which have run up large bills without people realising.

q.q: Why might you use airplane mode when playing a game on a phone?
o: To stop accidental purchases and contact with strangers
To make the game run faster and smoother on your phone
To unlock extra coins and free skins in the game
To save your game progress safely to the cloud
q.why: Airplane mode means you play offline, so no purchases or chat with strangers.

q.q: A gaming friend asks to add you on Instagram. What's the safest choice?
o: Accept, as you've played together for weeks
Give them your phone number instead
Accept, but keep your profile public
Keep them as a friend in the game only
q.why: Keep gaming friends in the game rather than adding them to your other social networks.

q.q: What is online gaming?
o: Playing a game on your own with no internet connection
Playing in real time with people across the world through a device
Playing a game that has been downloaded to your console
Buying games from an online shop
q.why: Online gaming means playing in real time with people across the world.

q.q: What percentage of children are gamers?
q.why: 91% of children are gamers.

q.q: How many hours a week does the average Fortnite player spend playing?
o: 1–2 hours
30–40 hours
6–10 hours
20–25 hours
q.why: The average Fortnite player spends 6–10 hours a week playing.

q.q: How can a parent stop surprise bills from in-game purchases on a console?
o: Let the child use the parent's bank card
Set up purchase controls such as a password for buying
Set the console to show adverts
Turn on the console's live chat
q.why: Ask a parent to set up purchase controls, for example a password for buying.

q.q: Another player keeps swearing at you in live chat. What should you do?
o: Keep playing and say nothing to anyone
Swear back so they stop
Give them your username on another app
Report the abusive chat and block the player
q.why: Learn how to report abusive chat and block anti-social players.

q.q: Why are gamers you meet online described as strangers?
o: They never use their real usernames
They play different games from you
Not everyone online is who they say they are
They always live in another country
q.why: Gamers you meet online are strangers: not everyone online is who they say they are.

q.q: A free game mod secretly lets a hacker into your computer. What type of malware is it?
o: A trojan
A worm
Pharming
Phishing
q.why: A trojan is disguised as something you want and opens a back door.

q.q: What is phishing?
o: Recording your key presses to steal passwords
Malware that spreads itself across a network
Secretly redirecting you from a real website to a fake copy
A fake email or message pretending to be a real organisation
q.why: Phishing tricks you with fake messages; pharming uses fake websites.

q.q: Someone's bank password is stolen after a hidden program records every key they press. What type of malware was this?
o: A trojan
A worm
Spyware (a keylogger)
Pharming
q.why: Spyware and keyloggers secretly record key presses to steal passwords and bank details.

q.q: Why is downloading films from illegal sites a problem?
o: It uses too much electricity
It is slower than streaming the film
It only works on school computers
It breaks copyright law and may carry malware
q.why: Illegal downloading breaks UK copyright law and can bring viruses or spyware.

q.q: What is pharming?
o: Illegally sharing music and films online
Secretly redirecting you from a real website to a fake copy
Sending fake emails that pretend to be from a bank
Malware that copies itself and slows a network
q.why: Pharming secretly redirects you to a fake website to capture your login details.

q.q: Which malware spreads itself from computer to computer across a network?
o: Spyware
A trojan
A worm
A keylogger
q.why: A worm spreads itself across a network, slowing everything down.

q.q: What is malware?
o: Any program that runs slowly
Software that has been downloaded legally
The name for all harmful (malicious) software
Software that protects you from viruses
q.why: Malware (malicious software) is the name for all harmful programs such as viruses, trojans, worms and spyware.

q.q: What does a keylogger record?
o: Your screen brightness
Your location
Your webcam
Your key presses
q.why: Spyware and keyloggers record your key presses to steal passwords and bank details.

q.q: You get an email that looks like it's from your bank asking you to confirm your password. What is this most likely to be?
o: A worm
Pharming
Phishing
Griefing
q.why: Fake messages pretending to be a real organisation to get your details are phishing.

q.q: Apart from downloads, how else can malware arrive?
o: Through emails, pop-ups, shared files and USB drives
Only through games bought in a shop
Only through websites that look unsafe
Only through printers and monitors
q.why: Malware can also arrive through emails, pop-ups, shared files, USB drives and connected devices.

q.q: What is the minimum age for most social networking sites?
q.why: Most social networks set 13 as the lower age limit.

q.q: Why should you turn off location services on social apps?
o: So your photos look clearer
So people can't see where you are
So the app uses less storage
So you can get more followers
q.why: Location sharing can let people find where you are.

q.q: What do tag approvals let you do?
o: Hide your location from your friends
Approve or dismiss tags before they appear on your profile
Tag anyone you like in your own photos
Delete posts that other people have shared
q.why: Tag approvals give you control over what you're linked to.

q.q: Why is it hard to take back a post?
o: Deleting a post costs money
Apps do not have a delete button
It may already have been copied and shared
Posts can never be edited after one minute
q.why: Once a post has been shared it's out of your control.

q.q: On Snapchat's Snap Map, what setting stops friends seeing where you are?
o: Private story
Airplane mode
Tag approvals
Ghost Mode
q.why: Snap Map shows friends where you are unless you turn on Ghost Mode.

q.q: What should your privacy settings be set to?
o: Friends of friends, so more people see you
Public, so you get the most followers
Whatever the app chose when you signed up
The strongest level, so only close friends can see your posts
q.why: Set privacy settings to the strongest level so only close friends can search for you, see or share your posts.

q.q: Which is a benefit of social networking?
o: Staying in touch with friends and sharing photos
Meeting strangers in person without telling anyone
Posting things that can never be deleted
Sharing your location with everyone
q.why: Social networks let you stay in touch, meet people with similar interests and share photos and videos.

q.q: Why can chatrooms and forums be risky?
o: They cost money to join
They connect strangers and may not be moderated
They only allow users over 18
They always share your location
q.why: Chatrooms and forums connect complete strangers and may not be moderated (checked).

q.q: Why do some people pressure others into sending inappropriate images online?
o: Behind a screen they feel bolder
Apps reward them with points
They are moderators checking content
They think it is required by the app
q.why: Behind a screen, some people feel bolder about pressuring others.

q.q: What is cyberbullying?
o: Repeatedly and deliberately harming someone using electronic devices
Spreading a computer virus to other people by email
Blocking someone who annoys you on a social network
Arguing with a friend once over who won a game online
q.why: Cyberbullying is repeated, deliberate harm using electronic devices.

q.q: Someone hacks a pupil's account and posts nasty messages as them. What form of cyberbullying is this?
o: Identity theft and impersonation
Trolling and harassment
Rejection and exclusion of the pupil
Defamation of their character
q.why: Hacking into someone's account and posting as them is identity theft and impersonation.

q.q: A user keeps posting deliberately angering comments under a news video just to start arguments. What is this called?
o: Griefing
Phishing
Trolling
Defamation
q.why: Trolling is posting inflammatory comments to disrupt a conversation and cause upset.

q.q: How can 'anonymous' cyberbullies often be traced?
o: Using their avatar
Using their username
They can never be traced
Using their IP address
q.why: Every device online has an IP address, which police and CEOP can use.

q.q: What is defamation?
o: Making a fake account in someone's name
Spreading untrue rumours that damage someone's reputation
Leaving someone out of a group chat
Posting someone's private photos
q.why: Defamation is spreading untrue rumours that damage a reputation.

q.q: A group deliberately leaves one pupil out of their group chat and games. Which form of cyberbullying is this?
o: Defamation
Rejection and exclusion
Threats and intimidation
Harassment and stalking
q.why: Deliberately leaving someone out of group chats or games is rejection and exclusion.

q.q: Why can cyberbullying feel worse than bullying in the playground?
o: It always stops when you log off
It only happens during school hours
It can only be seen by the bully
It can happen 24/7 and follow you into your home
q.why: Cyberbullying can happen 24/7 and follows you into your home through your phone.

q.q: What does it mean that cyberbullying can 'escalate'?
o: The bully moves to a different app
Other people join in, so it comes from many people
The messages are deleted automatically
The bullying stops after a short time
q.why: It can escalate quickly as other people join in.

q.q: Someone repeatedly sends a pupil unwanted, threatening messages. Which form of cyberbullying is this?
o: Defamation
Identity theft
Rejection and exclusion
Harassment and stalking
q.why: Repeatedly sending offensive, threatening or unwanted messages is harassment and stalking.

q.q: What helps track down cyberbullies?
o: Changing your username and saying nothing
Keeping evidence and telling a trusted adult or the police
Replying to the bully to find out who they are
Deleting the messages so they can't spread
q.why: Keeping evidence and telling parents, teachers and the police helps track down bullies.

q.q: Which is a warning sign of online grooming?
o: Your teacher posts a homework reminder on Google Classroom
A game you play shows an advert for a new skin you can buy
Someone you've never met offers free game currency and asks to chat privately
Your gran leaves a comment on a holiday photo you posted last week
q.why: Gifts plus moving to private chat are classic grooming signs.

q.q: Are online groomers always strangers?
o: Yes, unless they are under 18
No, they can be people the child already knows
No, they are always family members
Yes, they are always strangers
q.why: Groomers may be people already met through family or activities.

q.q: Someone you met in a game asks to meet you in Enniskillen on Saturday. What should you do?
o: Go, but bring a friend with you
Ask them for a photo first to check
Don't go, and tell a trusted adult
Go, but meet in a busy public place
q.why: Never agree to meet an online contact; tell a trusted adult.

q.q: Which of these would count as inappropriate content for a young person?
o: A revision page on BBC Bitesize
A chat room where nobody removes unsuitable comments
A video of a school concert
A recipe for pancakes
q.why: Unsupervised chats where nobody removes unsuitable comments are listed as inappropriate content.

q.q: What is online grooming?
o: Posting inflammatory comments online to start arguments and upset people
Deliberately spoiling other players' games through harassment or cheating
Building an emotional connection with a young person to exploit or abuse them
Changing your profile picture so that you look older than you really are
q.why: Grooming is befriending a young person and building an emotional connection to lower their guard.

q.q: Why do groomers often move a chat to private messaging?
o: Because private chat is faster
So nobody else can see what they say
Because public chats cost money
So the child can block them more easily
q.why: Groomers try to move the chat from open platforms to private messaging, away from others.

q.q: What is a good way to save a worrying online conversation?
o: Reply asking them to stop
Copy it out by hand and delete the original
Take screenshots, as they can be used as evidence
Forward it to all your friends
q.why: Screenshots can be used as evidence.

q.q: Which website can you use to report someone who is trying to meet up with a child?
o: CEOP
Google Classroom
MySchool
Snap Map
q.why: You can report to CEOP (Child Exploitation and Online Protection).

q.q: You see something online that upsets you. What should you do?
o: Close it, don't share it and tell a trusted adult
Leave it open so you can show it later
Reply to the person who posted it
Share it so your friends can warn others
q.why: Close it, don't share it, and tell a trusted adult. It is never your fault.

q.q: What is a digital footprint?
o: The amount of storage your files take up
Your profile picture on a social network
The trail of information left by everything you do online
A record of how many steps you walk each day
q.why: A digital footprint is the often permanent trail left by your online interactions.

q.q: You have 100 friends and each has 500 friends. How many 'friends of friends' could see your post?
q.why: 100 × 500 = 50,000; adding them (600) or a wrong place value are common slips.

q.q: What can a poor digital reputation affect?
o: Only the games you can play online
Only what adverts you are shown
Friendships, relationships and job prospects
Only how fast your phone works
q.why: A poor digital reputation can affect friendships, relationships and job prospects.

q.q: What does the T in THINK stand for?
o: Tagged
Typed
Trending
True
q.why: THINK: Is it True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind?

q.q: What is your digital reputation?
o: A score given to you by a social network
How people see you because of your online behaviour and posts
The trail of data your phone uses each month
The number of followers you have on social media
q.why: Your digital reputation is defined by your behaviour online and the content you post.

q.q: What does the K in THINK stand for?
o: Kept
Known
Kind
Key
q.why: THINK: True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind.

q.q: Why are real 'friends of friends' numbers usually smaller than the calculation suggests?
o: Posts are deleted after a day
Social networks limit you to 100 friends
Friend groups overlap
Most people have no friends online
q.why: Real numbers are smaller because friend groups overlap, but a post can still spread far.

q.q: Why can a digital footprint often be permanent?
o: Only the police can delete posts
Your phone stores everything forever
Social networks never let you delete anything
Once something has been sent, you lose control over it
q.why: Once something has been sent, you lose control over it.

q.q: Which guideline helps protect your digital reputation?
o: Accept every friend request you get
Use a real photo of yourself as your profile picture
Never post unacceptable comments online
Keep your profile public
q.why: Never post unacceptable comments, keep your profile private and use an avatar.

q.q: Why should you NOT delete upsetting messages?
o: Deleting them uses up data
They will delete themselves anyway
They might be funny later on
They can be used as evidence
q.why: Saved messages and screenshots are evidence that police and school can use.

q.q: What is Childline's phone number?
q.why: Childline is 0800 1111; 999 is for immediate danger.

q.q: Which organisation should you report to if an adult online is trying to meet up with a young person?
o: Your internet provider
CEOP
Google
Childline
q.why: CEOP (Child Exploitation and Online Protection) is the place to report anyone trying to meet up with a child.

q.q: Someone sends you threatening messages. What should you NOT do?
o: Tell a trusted adult at home
Reply with threats of your own
Save the messages as evidence
Report the account on the app
q.why: Never reply or retaliate: it makes things worse.

q.q: If you think someone is in immediate danger, what number should you call?
q.why: If someone is in immediate danger, call 999.

q.q: What are the four steps to follow if something online makes you uncomfortable, in order?
o: Delete it, block them, tell a friend, forget it
Tell a friend, reply, delete, report it
Reply, screenshot, delete, report it
Don't delete, don't reply, tell a trusted adult, report it
q.why: Don't delete (evidence), don't reply, tell a trusted adult, then report it.

q.q: Niamh gets nasty messages from an account. Her first idea is to block and delete everything. What should she do first?
o: Reply to ask why
Delete her own account
Share the messages with her class
Save the evidence
q.why: Don't just block and delete straight away. Save the evidence first!

q.q: Why does replying to bullies or trolls make things worse?
o: It reports your own account
It deletes the original messages
It sends them your IP address
It can escalate things and make an investigation harder
q.why: Replying makes things worse and can make an investigation harder.

q.q: Which of these is one of the nine tips for staying safe online?
o: Block people who make you feel uncomfortable
Accept friend requests to be polite
Keep your privacy settings at the default level
Share your school name so friends can find you
q.why: Block or ignore people who make you feel uncomfortable; never share personal details.

q.q: What is the maximum length of the e-safety video?
o: 30 seconds
10 minutes
5 minutes
2 minutes
q.why: The video must be no longer than 2 minutes.

q.q: What should you submit at the end of the video project?
o: The exported video, e.g. an MP4
The video editor project file
A screenshot of the finished video
The storyboard only
q.why: Export the finished video in a suitable format such as MP4, not the project file.

q.q: Why are feedback and evaluation important?
o: They decide which team member gets the marks
They let you judge progress and plan improvements
They replace the need to test the video
They make the finished video longer
q.why: They show progress, strengths, areas for development and what to improve next time.

q.q: Which is the safest way to get music for your video?
o: Use royalty-free music and credit it
Rip a song from YouTube with a converter site
Copy a song from the charts
Record a song from the radio
q.why: Royalty-free music respects copyright; converter sites break rules and are full of malware.

q.q: In the team, what is the Researcher's job?
o: Builds the project in a video editor
Finds the facts and gathers suitable images
Plans the storyboard and the look of the video
Adds transitions, audio and effects
q.why: The Researcher finds facts and images; the Designer plans the storyboard.

q.q: Which folders should you create inside your E SAFETY folder?
o: Images, Video Assets and Audio
My Pictures, My Music and Desktop
Researcher, Designer and Creator
Draft, Final and Old
q.why: Create E SAFETY with subfolders Images, Video Assets and Audio.

q.q: Which is an example of a good evaluation comment?
o: I liked our colour scheme, but next time I'd keep all the text boxes the same style
Our video was really good and everyone in our group liked it a lot
It was finished on time and it played on the computer when we tested it
The other teams' videos were not as good as ours, so we should get the top mark
q.why: A good evaluation is both positive and critical.

q.q: How many people are in each video team?
o: Two
Five
Three
Four
q.why: You work in a team of three.
